title: Indexes, Query Plans & ACID Transactions
summary: Why a B-tree index turns a full table scan into a fast search, how to read EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN, and how transactions keep multi-step changes all-or-nothing.
takeaways: Without a usable index, the database scans every row. An index lets it search a sorted structure instead.
Composite index column order matters: equality columns first, then the range column.
Keyset pagination (WHERE id > last_id) stays fast on deep pages; OFFSET re-reads every skipped row.
A transaction makes several writes atomic. Commit them all, or roll back to exactly where you started.

steps.label: BEGIN
steps.detail: Open a transaction. Nothing is visible to others until commit.

steps.label: Validate
steps.detail: Read the source balance and raise if there isn't enough.

steps.label: Debit source
steps.detail: UPDATE … SET qty = qty − n, using parameters, never string formatting.

steps.label: Credit destination
steps.detail: INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, so a missing row is created.

steps.label: COMMIT or ROLLBACK
steps.detail: Success makes both writes durable. Any error undoes both.

terms.definition: A balanced, sorted tree of key values pointing at rows, so lookups and range scans take logarithmic time.
An index that contains every column a query needs, so the table itself isn't read.
The strategy the database picks to execute a query, shown by EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN.
Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: the guarantees a database transaction provides.
Paging by remembering the last key seen (WHERE id > ?) instead of skipping rows with OFFSET.
An attack where untrusted input is pasted into SQL text. Parameterized queries prevent it.
